title: Episode 329: Edward VII: The Peacemaker, the Entente Cordiale, the Edwardian Summer, and the House of Saxe-Coburg-Gotha
description:
The glamorous, hedonistic, and diplomatically brilliant nine-year reign of King Edward VII. Kept out of state affairs for nearly sixty years by an overbearing Queen Victoria, 'Bertie' lived as a wealthy playboy, leading international society in Paris, Biarritz, and Ascot, surrounded by glamorous mistresses like Alice Keppel. Ascending the throne at fifty-nine in 1901, Edward astonished skeptics with his diplomatic genius. Visiting Paris in 1903, his charismatic charm and fluent French won over a hostile populace, forging the historic Entente Cordiale with France that revolutionized European geopolitics. Discover the Peacemaker King of the Edwardian Summer.

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Kings and Queens of England series examines the sovereign who ushered Britain into the twentieth century: a legendary playboy who became one of history's most effective royal diplomats, forging the alliance with France that reshaped the world: King Edward VII. Here is George with the story of the Peacemaker.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: BERTIE THE PLAYBOY: THE LONG APPRENTICESHIP: 1841 TO 1901
Born in November 1841 at Buckingham Palace, Albert Edward, Prince of Wales—known to family and the world as 'Bertie'—was subjected to a crushing, militaristic educational curriculum devised by Prince Albert, designed to mold him into a philosophical prince. Bertie was neither academic nor studious; he hated books, preferred sports and cards, and when his father died in 1861 following their confrontation over Bertie's youthful indiscretion with an actress, Queen Victoria unfairly blamed Bertie for Albert's death, refusing to allow him to see government dispatch boxes for decades. In 1863, Bertie married the dazzlingly beautiful Danish princess Alexandra, establishing their residence at Marlborough House in London and Sandringham in Norfolk. Bertie became the undisputed leader of high European society: smoking twelve cigars and twenty cigarettes daily, dining on twelve-course meals, betting on horses, and conducting glamorous affairs with society beauties like actress Lillie Langtry, Daisy Greville, Countess of Warwick, and his beloved final mistress, Alice Keppel. Bertie's long years as Prince of Wales had been a source of perpetual frustration: Queen Victoria refused to allow him access to official state papers or government cabinet discussions, believing him intellectually shallow, indiscreet, and hopelessly addicted to pleasure. Excluded from real power, the Prince channeled his boundless energy into creating a vibrant social court of his own at Sandringham House in Norfolk. He broke through old aristocratic prejudices, welcoming wealthy Jewish financiers like the Rothschilds and Sir Ernest Cassel into high society, patronizing horse racing at Ascot, and popularizing the luxurious culture of the weekend country house party. His genial warmth, impeccable manners, and cosmopolitan charm won the affection of the European capitals, even as moralists condemned his lavish lifestyle.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE DELAYED CORONATION AND APPENDICITIS MIRACLE: 1901 TO 1902
When Queen Victoria died in January 1901, fifty-nine-year-old Bertie ascended the throne as King Edward VII, choosing his grandfather's English name rather than Albert. The King moved swiftly to modernize the stuffy royal court, re-opening Buckingham Palace, throwing open state apartments, and instituting a dazzling new social era of open-topped motorcars, jazz, and country-house weekend parties. But disaster struck days before his scheduled coronation in June 1902: Edward collapsed at Windsor with agonizing abdominal pain. Royal surgeon Sir Frederick Treves diagnosed acute appendicitis and a perityphlitic abscess, warning the King that without immediate surgery he would die. Edward initially refused, insisting he could not disappoint his people. Treves firmly replied: 'Then, Sire, you will go to the Abbey as a corpse.' The operation was performed on a dining table inside Buckingham Palace; the abscess was drained, the King recovered miraculously, and on August 9, 1902, Edward VII was crowned at Westminster Abbey amid tremendous national relief. The appendicitis crisis on the eve of the 1902 coronation was a dramatic medical milestone. When the King collapsed in agonizing pain, Sir Frederick Treves performed an emergency operation to drain an abdominal abscess, a pioneering surgical intervention that saved Edward's life and brought modern appendectomy techniques into mainstream medical practice. When the delayed coronation finally took place at Westminster Abbey in August 1902, the eighty-year-old Archbishop of Canterbury, Frederick Temple, was so blind and frail that he placed St. Edward's Crown on the King's head backwards before nearly collapsing; King Edward tenderly helped the elderly prelate to his feet with regal patience. The nationwide celebration marked the joyful dawn of a colorful, modern monarchy.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE DIPLOMATIC MASTERPIECE: THE PARIS VISIT OF 1903
Edward VII's crowning achievement on the world stage came in May 1903 during his historic state visit to Paris. Following the Fashoda incident and British actions in the Boer War, French public opinion was fiercely anti-British: when Edward rode down the Champs-Élysées, crowds hissed, shouted 'Vivent les Boers!' and catcalled the King. Edward remained utterly unperturbed, smiling warmly, bowing to the crowd, and demonstrating his consummate mastery of French charm. At a gala performance at the Théâtre Français, during the interval, Edward approached the celebrated French actress Jeanne Granier in the foyer, gallantly kissing her hand and exclaiming in fluent French: 'Ah, Mademoiselle, I remember so well how I used to applaud you in London, where you represented all the grace and wit of France!' The Parisian audience was utterly charmed. By the third day of his visit, crowds lined the boulevards cheering 'Vive le Roi!' Edward's personal diplomacy transformed Anglo-French relations overnight. Edward VII's visit to Paris in May 1903 was one of the greatest diplomatic gambles in modern European history. Relations between Britain and France had been severely strained by the Fashoda Incident in Africa and intense French sympathy for the Boers during the South African war. When Edward arrived at the Gare du Bois de Boulogne, sullen crowds shouted insults and anti-British slogans. Undaunted, the King moved through the French capital with effortless savoir-faire: attending the theatre, praising French elegance, delivering flawless speeches in fluent French, and complimenting the famous actress Jeanne Granier with the memorable words: 'Ah, Madame, I remember how I applauded you in London!' By the time his train departed, the Parisian public had fallen completely under the spell of the charming English monarch.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE ENTENTE CORDIALE: APRIL 8, 1904
Edward's personal triumph in Paris opened the door for British Foreign Secretary Lord Lansdowne and French Foreign Minister Théophile Delcassé to negotiate the historic Entente Cordiale, signed on April 8, 1904. The treaty resolved centuries of colonial rivalries across the globe: France recognized British supremacy in Egypt, while Britain recognized French influence in Morocco, settling disputes in Newfoundland, West Africa, Siam, and the New Hebrides. More fundamentally, the Entente Cordiale brought Great Britain out of its traditional 'splendid isolation', aligning the British Empire with France and paving the way for the Anglo-Russian Convention of 1907. This diplomatic alignment created the Triple Entente, establishing a powerful balance of power against the aggressive military ambitions of Imperial Germany under Edward's nephew, Kaiser Wilhelm II, earning Edward the international title 'Edward the Peacemaker'. The signing of the Entente Cordiale in April 1904 marked a historic diplomatic realignment that ended nearly a thousand years of Anglo-French military rivalry. By resolving lingering colonial disputes over Egypt, Morocco, Newfoundland fisheries, and Southeast Asia, the treaty created an enduring geopolitical partnership between the two great western European democracies. Edward's nephew, Kaiser Wilhelm II of Germany, viewed the Entente with paranoid fury, accusing his uncle of orchestrating a sinister 'encirclement' of the German Empire. Yet Edward's diplomatic shuttle diplomacy—visiting kings and presidents across Europe—aimed not for war, but for a stable, balanced continental peace that would protect British commercial prosperity.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE DREADNOUGHT AND THE NAVAL ARMS RACE
While Edward promoted European peace, he was keenly aware of the growing threat posed by Kaiser Wilhelm II's expansion of the German High Seas Fleet. Edward was an enthusiastic champion of Admiral Sir John 'Jacky' Fisher, the radical First Sea Lord who revolutionized naval warfare. In 1906, Britain launched HMS Dreadnought, the world's first all-big-gun, steam-turbine-powered battleship. Armed with ten twelve-inch guns and capable of twenty-one knots, Dreadnought rendered every existing battleship in the world obsolete overnight, sparking an intense naval arms race with Imperial Germany. Edward maintained close personal interest in his armed forces, supporting the Haldane Army Reforms that created the British Expeditionary Force (BEF) and the Territorial Army, ensuring Britain was militarily prepared for the looming European crisis. The naval revolution spurred by King Edward VII and Admiral John Fisher fundamentally altered modern naval warfare. When HMS Dreadnought slipped into the water at Portsmouth in 1906, armed with ten twelve-inch guns and revolutionary steam turbine engines, it instantly rendered every other battleship afloat obsolete, forcing the German Imperial Navy into an exhausting and ruinous shipbuilding race. Simultaneously, Secretary of State for War Richard Haldane reorganized the British Army into an agile, highly trained Expeditionary Force of six infantry divisions supported by the newly created Territorial Army. King Edward took a passionate personal interest in military modernization, personally inspecting units, ensuring that Britain possessed an elite professional force capable of defending European liberty.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE CONSTITUTIONAL CRISIS AND THE 'PEOPLE'S BUDGET': 1909 TO 1910
The final year of Edward VII's reign was consumed by an explosive domestic constitutional crisis. In 1909, Liberal Chancellor David Lloyd George introduced the radical 'People's Budget', proposing progressive taxes on the wealth and land of aristocrats to fund social welfare programs, old age pensions, and the construction of new Dreadnought battleships. In an unprecedented move that shattered two centuries of constitutional precedent, the hereditary, Tory-dominated House of Lords vetoed the finance bill. Prime Minister H. H. Asquith introduced a Parliament Bill to permanently strip the House of Lords of its veto power over money bills. When the Lords resisted, Asquith approached the King, demanding a royal pledge to create hundreds of new Liberal peers to force the bill through, echoing the crisis of 1832. Edward was deeply distressed by the political warfare, attempting in vain to broker a compromise between the warring parties. The constitutional crisis provoked by David Lloyd George's 'People's Budget' in 1909 shook the British establishment to its core. The radical budget introduced progressive income taxes, land taxes, and estate duties on wealthy aristocrats to fund old-age pensions and naval rearmament. When the conservative majority in the House of Lords took the unprecedented, unconstitutional step of vetoing the budget, Prime Minister H.H. Asquith called a general election and demanded the power to create hundreds of Liberal peers to crush the Lords' veto. Edward VII was deeply troubled by the prospect of packing the House of Lords, arguing that such a radical step should only occur after a second general election. The fierce political warfare placed immense emotional stress on the aging, ailing King.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE PASSING OF THE PEACEMAKER: MAY 1910
In the spring of 1910, King Edward VII's lifelong chain-smoking caught up with him. Suffering from severe chronic bronchitis and emphysema, the sixty-eight-year-old king suffered a series of heart attacks at Buckingham Palace. On Friday, May 6, 1910, refusing to take to his bed, the King sat in an armchair in his frock coat, insisting: 'I shall not give in; I shall go on; I shall work to the end.' That afternoon, his racehorse Witch of the Air won at Kempton Park; when his son George informed him of the victory, Edward murmured his final words: 'I am very glad.' That night, with Queen Alexandra graciously permitting Alice Keppel to say her farewells, King Edward VII died peacefully. His funeral was the grandest gathering of European royalty in world history: nine reigning kings rode on horseback behind his coffin through London. Historian Barbara Tuchman famously observed that the pageant was the sunset of the old world, the final, dazzling summer before Europe plunged into the cataclysm of the First World War. On May 6, 1910, as Edward VII lay dying at Buckingham Palace from acute bronchitis and repeated heart attacks, he learned that his horse Witch of the Air had won at Kempton Park. Smiling weakly, the King whispered his final words to his son George: 'Yes, I have heard of it. I am very glad.' His funeral was the greatest gathering of European royalty in world history: nine reigning kings, led by his successor George V and Kaiser Wilhelm II, rode behind the gun carriage carrying Edward's coffin through London, followed by his beloved fox terrier Caesar. Historians look back on the nine-year reign of Edward VII as a golden Indian summer—an era of peace, elegance, and progressive reform before the dark clouds of World War I descended.
